I can't fathom how immature a person has to be to object to these rules.
What's immature about seeking out clear (i.e. not the "i know it when i see it" type) rules?

Your question must include a question mark.

Why on earth is this stupid, counter-productive, unpopular and unnecessary rule still here?

I think leaving the wording as "must include a question mark" is more trouble than it's worth. Any post that gets saved from deletion under the leniency period but doesn't have a question mark runs the risk of being spammed with reports, shouted down, or downvoted into oblivion over what amounts to semantics.

Consider changing the wording to strongly suggest using a question mark and note that anything that doesn't trigger the leniency period will be deleted. I think it would save some trouble in the long run and accomplishes the same end.

So, a few thoughts. (Or a whole lot of thoughts, this is probably the longest post I've ever written, both here and on Reddit... Originally I was only going to make a few comments, but it kinda expanded.)
Also, my formatting doesn't seem to work all that well here, sorry.

Rule #1 needs some work, or at least a more rigorous explanation to go along with it:
* First things first, the question mark requirement is a problem. Even if it did serve some purpose at one point, it is now so universally criticized and despised that you will never hear the end of the issues with it.
* Secondly, I think the "must include a question and nothing else" is a little strict. If I want to ask something like, "Gun to your head, would you have sex with Steve Buscemi" my post would (seemingly) qualify for deletion as it includes context that should be posted in the discussion thread.
* It may also limit the potential for a thread which is asking for responses to a set of questions. I can ask, "Who are you voting for in the upcoming election and why?" in a concise manner whilst asking two separate questions, I think making a thread titled "The Hillary Clinton controversy" is reasonable so long as it contains a question (or set of them) in the text of the post, even though a better title would be "What's the deal with this Hillary Clinton stuff?" I would suggest that the post MUST contain a question in EITHER the title OR the text, but that a reminder/suggestion be given about the title, if it's the latter.
* Finally, an answer may be required in order to provide the necessary context for the question itself. If a person is wondering who makes the best chocolate, they may wish to include their own answer and reasoning in the original post to provide content for people to respond to. As a post gains traction, the reply of the OP may get lost under the other replies. While I don't think this specific issue is something that threads would be deleted for, I also know that the community on the site is VERY upset about excessive moderation without need, so it bears mentioning.

Rule #2: I think this rule is relatively (concerns below) good in theory, by which I mean if applied objectively. However, the inability for most people to do that is a pretty fundamental flaw of humanity.
* Soapboxing/Grandstanding and Marketing/Agenda. I'd almost rather people make their agenda apparent in the question itself. If an activist is phrasing their question as your latter examples but still includes all the Nestle stuff in the text of their post, they are still trying to push their agenda. You can't stop people from trying when accounts are free and posts easy, and trying is a very dangerous game. You will never, ever be able to enforce this policy fairly, nor without controversy. I believe that flagging posts with flair (similar to what /v/news does for Misleading Titles and the like) that seem to push an agenda or break this rule is a relatively hands-off enforcement of this policy. If a single user has repeated infractions against the rule (especially for the same issue/event they are posting about) then deletion becomes a more viable solution, however making it obvious that this is the reason is important.
* Self-promotion. Basically, if someone isn't trying to sell something, or at least isn't OBVIOUSLY only posting for profit, don't delete it. There's plenty of independent people on the site who want to grab some attention for their project, hobby, or even product. Really, how many problems have there been with posts that would break this part of the rule? How is deleting a question that actually features CONTENT a good thing? Seriously, half of things lately are just bullshit or circlejerk posts.

Since I'm going in order, I'll just say that I think **Rule #3 **is pretty reasonable. While there are a few things I could potentially see as having link posts (a straw poll or similar was my immediate thought) I see no reason why this wouldn't be at least equally appropriate in the text of a self-post.

The leniency period. I think it's a good policy, but there's something I'd add. An individual should not be able to repeatedly ignore the rules just because their post got a few replies each time, or they posted it in the middle of the night. I would add a strikes policy. If a person makes a post that falls under the leniency period, they get a warning. If they get 3, or 5, or however many warnings for breaking the same rule, their post is deleted EVEN IF IT FALLS UNDER THE LENIENCY PERIOD, or maybe after an extended period. Say, if a person has made 5 posts that are promoting their website selling wristbands, maybe that post gets deleted anyways, or can be deleted for up to 3 hours and/or until it has 15 comments, something like that. Additionally, the leniency period should cover any post made after a rule change. If you add a rule, give people warnings for a week or so, before it falls under general enforcement stuff. I also think a "views" criterion would be fitting. If something has received 500 views, it's still high-traffic even if not many have replied to it. Especially for questions that might have long-form responses, such as how complex political posts or science-y things sometimes are.

Other thoughts:
I think the inclusion of post tagging (flairs) could allow mods to highlight posts that do break the rules but might not warrant deletion, or fall in the leniency policy.

I also know that the community on the site is VERY upset about excessive moderation without need, so it bears mentioning.

I want to repeat and emphasize this, because I think it's the single most important thing for the mods to remember, and I strongly suspect that the mods on this sub, perplexing though that might be, still don't fully grasp this fact.

Deletion, on a forum, is the equivalent of imprisonment in the justice system. It's a penalty that's applied to threads or posts that pose such a grave danger to the forum that they cannot responsibly be left in place - threads or posts that must be removed for the good of the community. And that requires that the thread or post not only pose a threat to the community, but that it be obvious that it does - if there's any doubt, then it does not rise to a sufficient level to justify deletion. It's a standard akin to the justice system's presumption of "innocent until proven guilty." A thread or post should be treated as harmless unless and until it can effectively be proven that it's harmful, and only then should it be deleted.

No other threads or posts should ever be deleted. Period.

I think this community and these mods would be well served to keep that consideration in the forefront when considering rules.

But here's the thing though. Not everyone agrees with your interpretation of how mods should function. I actually don't, myself, but that's not why we are here. I'm fine with most sub moderation so long as the rules are reasonable, since (as we've now seen) alternative subs can be created and run however they want.

In general the rules sound reasonable, but as a point of note...

I think this should say "stylistically correct" - punctuation really isn't part of grammar, it's intended to remove ambiguity and create tone. If you do keep it though, it would be worth correcting the spelling (there's a second m in grammatically).
